n: The Lord provides safety to anyone seeking his protection. The psalmist trusts and submits to the Lord. See also {{Psalm 71:1-3|Psalm 71:1–3}}.

The psalmist urges the faithful to seek safety in the Lord and wait for his salvation. After experiencing something like death, he shares how the Lord remained faithful. This psalm points ahead to the suffering of Jesus ({{Luke 23:46|Luke 23:46}}).
The psalmist urgently asks the Lord to notice his desperate situation ({{Psalm 71:2|PSalms 71:2}}; {{Psalm 88:2|88:2}}; {{Psalm 102:2|102:2}}).
*Into Your hands I commit my spirit*: The psalmist will trust his Lord, whether he lives or dies. Jesus said these words on the cross before he died ({{Luke 23:46|Luke 23:46}}).
Trusting the Lord means believing he cares about our well-being.
*in the open*: This means a wide area, unlike a narrow or tight place that causes distress (see {{Psalm 18:19|Psalm 18:19}}).

In this prayer for mercy, the psalmist places a description of his intense suffering and the pain of rejection between two statements of trust in the Lord ({{Psalm 31:6|Psalm 31:6}}, {{Psalm 31:14|14}}).
*my bones are wasting away*: This phrase powerfully describes how despair can harm our physical health.
Hope does not trust weak and unreliable human beings. It trusts only in the Lord. The suffering person places his life in God’s hands while he waits for the Lord to bring justice.
*My times are in Your hands*: To give up control of timing is one way to express submission.
The psalmist, who did not deserve to be disgraced, invokes the principle of retribution (see study note on Psalm 1:6; see also “Prayers for Vengeance” Theme Note).
The psalmist, who did not deserve to be disgraced, invokes the principle of retribution
The psalmist thanks the Lord for answering his prayer and rescuing him ({{Psalm 31:1-18|Psalm 31:1–18}}).
*Blessed be the LORD*: The psalmist expresses his joy at the experience of God’s goodness and love. Throughout his struggles, the Lord has cared for him.

Out of his own pain and renewed awareness of the Lord’s goodness, the psalmist turns to others who suffer. He holds out the promise of God’s loving care for those who persevere in hoping for the Lord.

The Lord’s forgiveness brings people back into a relationship with him, removes their guilt, and gives them joy. Paul quoted this text when explaining justification by faith alone ({{Romans 4:4-8|Romans 4:4–8}}).

This wisdom psalm of confession and thanks urges the godly to learn from the psalmist’s journey through sin, denial, confession, and forgiveness. The early church used this psalm as one of the seven penitential psalms (psalms of repentance, see also {{Psalm 6:1-10|Psalms 6}}, {{Psalm 38:1-22|38}}, {{Psalm 51:1-19|51}}, {{Psalm 102:1-28|102}}, {{Psalm 130:1-8|130}}, {{Psalm 143:1-12|143}}).

The psalmist admits his sin (see {{Psalm 19:12-13|Psalms 19:12–13}}; {{Psalm 25:7|25:7}}, {{Psalm 25:11|11}}, {{Psalm 25:15-22|15–22}}) and his resistance to confessing sin. The Lord pressed him hard until he confessed his guilt.
The psalmist believes his suffering comes directly from the Lord's discipline (compare {{Psalm 38:2|Psalms 38:2}}; {{Psalm 39:10|39:10}}).

God has forgiven the guilt and rebellion mentioned in {{Psalm 32:1|Psalm 32:1}}. The Lord’s nature is to reconcile and forgive ({{Psalm 78:38|Psalms 78:38}}; {{Psalm 85:2|85:2}}; {{Psalm 130:4|130:4}}), but he requires people to confess and repent.
The godly will learn from the psalmist’s experience to pray for forgiveness before it is too late.
The Lord promises to be a safe place for his people ({{Psalm 31:20|Psalm 31:20}}). Instead of feeling terrified ({{Psalm 31:13|Psalm 31:13}}), the psalmist hears songs of victory all around.
God interrupts the psalmist's teaching with a message inviting the godly to receive the Lord's wisdom (see {{Psalm 5:8|Psalms 5:8}}; {{Psalm 23:3|23:3}}; {{Psalm 25:4-6|25:4–6}}).
The foolish person lacks wisdom. Ignoring the Lord’s advice harms life and makes a person like an animal (see {{Isaiah 1:3|Isaiah 1:3}}; {{James 3:3|James 3:3}}).
Difficulties common to all of life will come to the wicked, whereas the Lord promises to protect the godly with his care.
The psalmist urges the godly to praise the Lord with melodies, with a new song, and with skillfully-played music.

This hymn of creation (see also {{Psalm 8:1-9|Psalms 8}}, {{Psalm 19:1-14|19}}, {{Psalm 104:1-35|104}}, {{Psalm 145:1-21|145}}) might be a continuation of {{Psalm 32:1-11|Psalm 32}}. It urges readers to praise God ({{Psalm 33:1-3|Psalm 33:1–3}}), to recognize the power of his word in creation ({{Psalm 33:4-7|33:4–7}}), and to respect the Creator ({{Psalm 33:8-11|33:8–11}}). It gives hope to forgiven sinners ({{Psalm 32:1-11|Psalm 32}}) that they can live a new life in the fear of the Lord and under divine protection.
God's word shows his character and power.
The nations surrounding Israel thought that the sea had divine power, but it is under God’s control, within boundaries that he set (see {{Psalm 104:8-10|Psalm 104:8–10}}).
The power of the Lord extends to all the nations (see Psalm 22; {{Psalm 96:1-3|96:123}}).
Fear of the Lord begins with awe for God and for his powerful word. His word created everything and continues to order and sustain creation. He frustrates the plans of people who oppose his will.
The plans of powerful people will only succeed if God allows it (see {{Isaiah 8:9-10|Isaiah 8:9210}}).

- God’s word still orders creation and will do so forever.

- God's purposes are wonderful ({{Psalm 40:5|Psalms 40:5}}; {{Psalm 92:5|92:5}}).
People who fear God are chosen as his inheritance (see {{Psalm 33:13-19|Psalm 33:13–19}}). This does not include rebellious people ({{Psalm 78:62|Psalm 78:62}}).
From the heavens, the Lord searches out and cares for anyone who fears him (see {{Psalm 14:2-3|Psalm 14:2–3}}).
*army …great strength. … horse*: Even military power is under God's control (see {{Psalm 33:10-11|Psalm 33:10–11}}; {{Ecclesiastes 9:11|Ecclesiastes 9:11}}).
God watches over all who live by his counsel ({{Psalm 32:8|Psalm 32:8}}). He protects, rescues, and stays close to them ({{Psalm 34:15-22|Psalm 34:15–22}}).
The faithful see God's power in creation and world events. They respond with trust, commitment, joy, and hope as they pray and wait for God's help.
The psalmist uses wordplay to contrast his people's certain hope (Hebrew *yakhal*) in the Lord with the supposed strength (Hebrew *khayil*) of the wicked's horses.
Abimelech is another name for Achish (see {{1 Samuel 21:10-15|1 Samuel 21:10–15}}). The body of the psalm makes no explicit connection to this event.
The psalmist encourages those in need to join him in praise.

This wisdom psalm includes a thanksgiving song of praise ({{Psalm 34:1-7|Psalm 34:1–7}}) that celebrates the Lord for caring for and protecting godly sufferers. It also includes an invitation to wisdom ({{Psalm 34:8-14|Psalm 34:8–14}}) and explains wisdom concerning the Lord’s care for the needy and the suffering of the wicked ({{Psalm 34:15-22|Psalm 34:15–22}}).
The psalmist describes his experiences of answered prayer.

The *angel of the LORD* showed God's presence during the journey through the wilderness. He protected Israel from Egypt's forces ({{Exodus 14:19-20|Exodus 14:19–20}}), and he will guard all those who are godly ({{Psalm 91:11|Psalm 91:11}}).
The godly encourage everyone to seek wisdom, to fear the Lord, and to place themselves under the protection of the Lord’s angel.
Fear of the Lord includes reverence and respect, and it motivates a life of wisdom (see {{Proverbs 1:7|Proverbs 1:7}}; {{Proverbs 9:10|9:10}}).
Anyone who listens, even children, can become wise followers of God.

Wisdom has three parts: 

- fearing the Lord ({{Psalm 34:11|Psalm 34:11}}),

- doing good ({{Psalm 34:14|Psalm 34:14}}), and

- rejecting evil ({{Psalm 34:13|Psalm 34:13}}).
Peter quotes this passage in his instructions for peaceful living ({{1 Peter 3:10-12|1 Peter 3:10–12}}).
Godly people choose their words carefully. Speaking evil and telling lies is unwise (see {{Psalm 10:7|Psalm 10:7}}; compare {{Psalm 17:1|17:1}}).
The way of peace leads to harmony and order, whereas evil destroys them (see {{Psalm 37:11|Psalm 37:11}}).

The Lord distinguishes between wise and foolish people; he shows his concern for the wise by rescuing them from trouble ({{Psalm 34:15|Psalm 34:15}}, {{Psalm 34:17-20|17–20}}). However, God destroys the foolish ({{Psalm 34:16|Psalm 34:16}}, {{Psalm 34:21|21}}).

Those who are brokenhearted have a spirit of deep sorrow for sin and a strong dependence on the Lord. God accepts this humble spirit as a proper sacrifice ({{Psalm 51:17|Psalm 51:17}}). The wicked hate people who are brokenhearted ({{Psalm 109:16|Psalm 109:16}}). But the Lord heals them and restores them ({{Psalm 147:3|Psalm 147:3}}; see {{Isaiah 57:15|Isaiah 57:15}}; {{Isaiah 61:1|61:1}}).

The godly might suffer, but the Lord will reward them in the end. Similarly, the wicked might prosper for a time, but ultimately they will perish ({{Psalm 1:6|Psalms 1:6}}; {{Psalm 34:15-16|34:15–16}}).

- Bones represent a person's whole self (see {{Psalm 6:2|Psalm 6:2}}). 

- *not one of them will be broken*: John applied this statement to Jesus at the crucifixion ({{John 19:36|John 19:36}}).
In this lament, the Lord's troubled servant asks God to notice his situation and defend him.
The psalmist desires the Lord's salvation. The language may seem harsh, but it comes from a wish for justice and for the Lord to help the needy and oppressed.

- A *dark and slick* path suggests instability and sudden disaster under the Lord's judgment (see {{Psalm 69:23|Psalms 69:23}}; {{Psalm 73:18|73:18}}; {{Psalm 82:5|82:5}}; {{Psalm 107:10|107:10}}; {{Psalm 143:3|143:3}}). 

- The *angel of the LORD* is an agent of judgment as well as salvation.
Nothing in the universe can compare with the Lord (see {{Psalm 86:8|Psalms 86:8}}; {{Psalm 89:6|89:6}}, {{Psalm 89:8|8}}; {{Isaiah 40:18|Isaiah 40:18}}, {{Isaiah 40:25|25}}).
False witnesses want nothing but violence (see {{Psalm 11:4-6|Psalms 11:4–6}}; {{Psalm 54:3|54:3}}).
The psalmist presents the Lord with the reasons for his suffering. Evil has many faces. He is tired and worn out, and he knows that only the Lord can help him.
The psalmist's attackers *gnashed their teeth* to show their jealousy.
John applied this claim of innocence (see also {{Psalm 69:4|Psalm 69:4}}) to Jesus ({{John 15:25|John 15:25}}).

In this prayer for justice, the psalmist faces a crisis so great that only the Lord can resolve it. The psalmist chooses the right path and believes that vengeance belongs to the Lord.

God’s patience allows the wicked to continue in their evil ways. Because of this, their hearts grow harder and they find reasons to justify their behavior.
*Aha, aha!*: This Hebrew word (*he’akh*) expresses a feeling of joy.
The psalmist calls on the Lord to judge the wicked and to rescue the godly and bring them joy.
*no fear of God*: Paul uses this phrase to describe how all people are morally corrupt ({{Romans 3:18|Romans 3:18}}).
Foolish people reject wisdom and goodness while they chase after evil.

This lament contrasts the foolish world made by the wicked with the wise world created and maintained by the Lord. The wicked care only about themselves, while the Lord cares for all creation. He will step in to bring justice to his world. The righteous will enjoy his protection, but the wicked will die.
God’s all-encompassing goodness surpasses that of the created order. God graciously meets his people’s practical needs.
As the source of wisdom, the Lord is reliable and incomparable. His faithful care extends to all parts of the created order.
All creatures live by God's grace ({{1 Timothy 4:10|1 Timothy 4:10}}).
God invites everyone to a feast in his house (compare {{Proverbs 9:1-6|Proverbs 9:1–6}}).
God's wisdom covers all of creation and protects those who follow him.
The psalmist is sure that the chaos caused by the wicked ({{Psalm 36:1-4|Psalm 36:1–4}}) will stop when they die.
*envy*: The jealous desire to have what others enjoy leads to further sin ({{Psalm 73:3|Psalm 73:3}}; {{Proverbs 3:31|Proverbs 3:31}}; {{James 1:14-15|James 1:14–15}}; {{James 4:1-2|4:1–2}}).

The wise respond to evil by trusting in the Lord. Trust has five parts:

- Do not become irritated or jealous of those who do evil ({{Psalm 37:1-2|Psalm 37:1–2}}).

- Delight in the Lord ({{Psalm 37:3-4|Psalm 37:3–4}}).

- Submit to the Lord ({{Psalm 37:5-6|Psalm 37:5–6}}).

- Practice patience in hope ({{Psalm 37:7|Psalm 37:7}}).

- Avoid anger ({{Psalm 37:8-9|Psalm 37:8–9}}).

This psalm addresses the issues raised in {{Psalm 36:1-12|Psalm 36}}: 

- How should the godly react to evil? 

- When will the Lord bring justice? 

- Why does he allow the wicked to harm his creation? 

{{Psalm 37:1-40|Psalm 37}} provides clear answers that reduce the tensions of life ({{Psalm 37:1-9|Psalm 37:1–9}}, {{Psalm 37:34|34}}) and promise that the meek will have a future ({{Psalm 37:10-11|Psalm 37:10–11}}, {{Psalm 37:39-40|39–40}}). 

The contrast between the godly and the wicked highlights the uselessness of foolishness ({{Psalm 37:12-24|Psalm 37:12–24}}, {{Psalm 37:27-33|27–33}}). The psalmist's personal insights add a human element ({{Psalm 37:25-26|Psalm 37:25–26}}, {{Psalm 37:35-38|35–38}}). He encourages viewing the land's inheritance with a long-term perspective: The earth belongs to the Lord, who will give it to those he blesses—the humble and godly who trust, hope, and follow him (see {{Psalm 37:9|Psalm 37:9}}, {{Psalm 37:11|11}}, {{Psalm 37:22|22}}, {{Psalm 37:29|29}}, {{Psalm 37:34|34}}; see also {{Isaiah 57:13|Isaiah 57:13}}; {{Matthew 5:5|Matthew 5:5}}).

Human life is limited and does not last long (see {{Psalm 90:5-6|Psalms 90:5–6}}; {{Psalm 92:7|92:7}}; {{Psalm 102:4|102:4}}, {{Psalm 102:11|11}}; {{Psalm 103:15|103:15}}; {{Psalm 129:6|129:6}}; {{Isaiah 40:7-8|Isaiah 40:7–8}}).
Doing good means developing a commitment to wisdom (see {{Psalm 34:14|Psalm 34:14}}; {{Proverbs 3:5-7|Proverbs 3:5–7}}).
Trusting in the Lord helps reduce irritability and envy ({{Psalm 37:1|Psalm 37:1}}).
To delight in the Lord means to follow the Lord’s ways and find joy in him.
Justice occurs when the Lord’s will triumphs and the godly experience his rescue ({{Isaiah 45:8|Isaiah 45:8}}; {{Isaiah 51:5-6|51:5–6}}; {{Isaiah 58:8|58:8}}, {{Isaiah 58:10-11|10–11}}).
*Be still*: We should let the Lord be God rather than taking matters into our own hands.

Irritability and anger can quickly damage a person’s character.

When someone becomes easily upset or angry, it affects the way that person thinks and acts. Over time, this can weaken good habits and harm relationships.

Learning patience and self-control helps protect and strengthen character.
The wicked will not possess the land; those who trust in the Lord will. The Lord promises an inheritance because he is committed to caring for his people.

The Lord creates peace ({{Psalm 85:10|Psalm 85:10}})—he brings peace to a chaotic world ({{Psalm 29:11|Psalm 29:11}}; {{Psalm 37:11|37:11}}; {{Psalm 85:8|85:8}}; {{Psalm 147:14|147:14}}). His wisdom leads the meek to peace ({{Psalm 119:165|Psalm 119:165}}; {{Matthew 5:5|Matthew 5:5}}).

The wicked show their envy by gnashing their teeth (an expression of anger and hostility). They make plans to harm the godly. But the Lord laughs at them because he knows they will fail ({{Psalm 2:4|Psalm 2:4}}).
The wicked seek to destroy the Lord’s order, but he defeats them.
The wicked prepare weapons, but those weapons will turn against them (compare {{Psalm 7:12-13|Psalm 7:12–13}}).
It is better to be wise with little money than to be rich and evil ({{Proverbs 15:16|Proverbs 15:16}}; {{Proverbs 16:8|16:8}}, {{Proverbs 16:19|19}}; {{Proverbs 17:1|17:1}}; {{Proverbs 28:6|28:6}}).
The Lord cares for the blameless in this life and for eternity, but the wicked will perish.
*Smoke* represents the temporary nature of life ({{Psalm 68:2|Psalm 68:2}}; {{Psalm 102:3|102:3}}).

- To borrow and never repay shows a dishonest way of life.

- Generous givers freely share what they freely receive from the Lord (see {{Psalm 111:5|Psalm 111:5}}; {{Psalm 112:5|112:5}}).
The honesty and strength of a godly person's life come from the Lord (see {{Proverbs 4:12|Proverbs 4:12}}; {{Proverbs 14:15|14:15}}; {{Proverbs 16:9|16:9}}; {{Proverbs 20:24|20:24}}).
The Lord does not abandon his children or their descendants.

The godly are wise; they do good and reject evil. The Lord cares for them, protecting them and ensuring that they receive their rightful portion of the land as their inheritance. The wicked might try to ambush the godly, but they will not succeed.
The righteous base their counsel on the Lord’s wisdom.
*The law of his God is in his heart*: The godly accept God’s instruction and live by it (see {{Psalm 119:11|Psalm 119:11}}; {{Jeremiah 24:7|Jeremiah 24:7}}; {{Jeremiah 31:31-34|31:31–34}}).
The wicked might appear to be flourishing like a tree (compare {{Psalm 52:8|Psalm 52:8}}; {{Psalm 92:12-13|92:12–13}}), but they eventually die and are forgotten ({{Psalm 37:2|Psalm 37:2}}).
The Lord provides strength for his people.
The meaning of this phrase is uncertain (also in {{Psalm 70:1|70:1}}).
The psalmist’s sins brought the Lord’s anger and rage. Because of this, the Lord disciplined and rebuked him, like arrows and blows striking him. As a result, his whole body is sick.
These verses introduce the psalmist's confession ({{Psalm 38:18|Psalm 38:18}}) and describe his miserable state.
This psalm is a lament and a prayer for healing. The psalmist's suffering is linked to his unconfessed sin. He admits his sin and trusts the Lord with his situation.

Sin can lead to sickness and even death ({{1 Corinthians 11:30|1 Corinthians 11:30}}). The psalmist may have felt physically ill, or his sickness was a metaphor for emotional distress. He understood it came from God and endangered his life (see {{Psalm 32:3|Psalms 32:3}}; {{Psalm 39:10|39:10}}).
The psalmist feels burdened because of sin (see {{Psalm 40:12|Psalms 40:12}}; {{Psalm 41:4|41:4}}; compare {{Genesis 4:13|Genesis 4:13}}).
The severity of God’s punishment brings anguish that affects every part of the psalmist’s being.
The psalmist wants to reconnect with God but feels distant. He feels lost and alone as his friends leave him.
The psalmist suffers quietly before his opponents (see {{Isaiah 53:7|Isaiah 53:7}}).
The Lord alone will resolve the conflict ({{Psalm 9:18|Psalms 9:18}}; {{Psalm 27:14|27:14}}; {{Psalm 37:9|37:9}}, {{Psalm 37:34|34}}).
The psalmist, unable to bear his suffering and close to collapse (compare {{Psalm 15:5|Psalm 15:5}}), admits his sin (see {{Psalm 32:5|Psalm 32:5}}).
The psalmist feels more pain because his enemies hate him for no reason.

In the Psalms, people often ask the Lord to act quickly in times of great need ({{Psalm 22:19|Psalms 22:19}}; {{Psalm 31:2|31:2}}; {{Psalm 40:13|40:13}}; {{Psalm 69:17|69:17}}; {{Psalm 70:1|70:1}}; {{Psalm 71:12|71:12}}; {{Psalm 79:8|79:8}}; {{Psalm 102:2|102:2}}; {{Psalm 141:1|141:1}}; {{Psalm 143:7|143:7}}). However, wisdom and experience show that God's people often need to wait for him to act ({{Psalm 27:14|Psalms 27:14}}; {{Psalm 37:7|37:7}}; {{Isaiah 8:17|Isaiah 8:17}}; {{Isaiah 40:31|40:31}}).
Jeduthun was a Levitical singer who was appointed by David, along with Asaph ({{1 Chronicles 9:16|1 Chronicles 9:16}}; {{1 Chronicles 16:38|16:38}}; {{1 Chronicles 25:1|25:1}}).
Suffering in silence makes the psalmist's anguish, pain, and inner distress worse.
This prayer for rescue shows the psalmist's discouragement, which comes from not fully understanding his situation.

*how fleeting my life is*: This perspective comes out of suffering (see {{Psalm 78:39|Psalms 78:39}}; {{Psalm 89:47-48|89:47–48}}; {{Psalm 90:3-10|90:3–10}}). The human lifetime is but a moment to God ({{Psalm 90:4|Psalm 90:4}}), as temporary as a breath (see {{Psalm 39:11|Psalms 39:11}}; {{Psalm 144:4|144:4}}).

Due to his suffering and sin, the psalmist concludes that life is meaningless and short (see {{Job 7:7-10|Job 7:7–10}}; {{Isaiah 40:6-8|Isaiah 40:6–8}}). He had expected only a wicked life to be like that (see {{Psalm 37:2|Psalms 37:2}}, {{Psalm 37:20|20}}; {{Psalm 103:15-16|103:15–16}}), but now it seems irrelevant whether a person is godly or not.
The idea that rebellion leads to suffering is a common theme in {{Psalm 32:1-11|Psalms 32}}, {{Psalm 38:1-41:13|38–41}}.
The psalmist links suffering with God’s discipline, assuming that it is punishment for his sin.

The Lord uses discipline to correct his children ({{Psalm 38:1|Psalms 38:1}}, {{Psalm 38:3|3}}, {{Psalm 38:7|7}}; {{Psalm 40:12|40:12}}; see {{Proverbs 3:11-12|Proverbs 3:11–12}}; {{Hebrews 12:5-6|Hebrews 12:5–6}}).
A *foreigner* could not own land (see {{Leviticus 25:23|Leviticus 25:23}}). The patriarchs had lived as guests in Canaan ({{Psalm 105:23|Psalm 105:23}}).
Earlier, the psalmist asked God to stay close to him ({{Psalm 38:21-22|Psalm 8:21–22}}). Now, he wants God to leave him alone. This is similar to how Job felt ({{Job 7:17-19|Job 7:17–19}}).
The psalmist thanks the Lord for rescue and affirms that people can trust God.

This psalm has a thanksgiving song ({{Psalm 40:1-10|Psalm 40:1–10}}) and a lament ({{Psalm 40:11-17|40:11–17}}). The thanksgiving song explains why the psalmist is thankful ({{Psalm 40:1-5|Psalm 40:1–5}}), shows a promise to stay committed ({{Psalm 40:6-8|40:6–8}}), and shares a public testimony about God's character ({{Psalm 40:7-10|40:7–10}}). The lament talks about the psalmist's troubles due to his sins ({{Psalm 40:11-12|Psalm 40:11–12}}) and includes two prayers asking for justice ({{Psalm 40:13-15|40:13–15}}, {{Psalm 40:17|17}}).

- The Lord delights in the attitude and character of the person giving an offering more than the offering itself. 

- *my ears You have opened*: The Greek text reads *You have given me a body.* In {{Hebrews 10:5-7|Hebrews 10:5–7}}, the writer quotes from the Greek version of {{Psalm 40:6-8|Psalm 40:6–8}}. He presents these words as something Jesus said when he left heaven and came into the world.
*it is written about me in the scroll*: Moses had recorded God’s requirements for Israel’s kings in {{Deuteronomy 17:14-15|Deuteronomy 17:14–15}}.
The psalmist prays that the Lord will be true to his character when answering this plea for mercy.

- The psalmist is troubled by both his adversities and his own sins and prays for rescue.

- This passage is almost the same as {{Psalm 70:1-5|Psalm 70}}.
